slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild Anscombe's quartet in pandas (the lesson's 4 mini-datasets with nearly identical mean/std/correlation) and render all 4 with seaborn's lmplot in a col_wrap grid, confirming by eye that the shapes differ (a real line, a curve, an outlier-driven fit, and a single-point leverage case) even though the summary numbers match to 2 decimals; then pick 3 real variables from any dataset you choose (one categorical breakdown, one trend over time, one relationship between two numbers) and write down, before coding, which chart type each one calls for and why.
slots.deliverable: A rendered 2x2 Anscombe's-quartet chart grid with the matching-stats table printed above it, plus a written chart-type decision (with one-sentence reasoning each) for 3 real variables from a dataset of your choice.

lessons.title: Misleading Charts & How to Avoid Them

slots.practicalActivity: Take one chart from the real dataset you picked last slot and build two deliberately broken versions: one with a truncated, non-zero-based y-axis that exaggerates a small difference, and one using a rainbow qualitative color scale on data that is actually ordered; then rebuild a clean, honest version applying the color/layout rules (one accent color, zero-based axis, minimal gridlines, a title that states the finding) and write 2-3 sentences per broken version explaining exactly how a reader would be misled.
slots.deliverable: Two deliberately misleading versions of the same real chart, one corrected honest version, and a written explanation of exactly what each misleading version distorts.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the object-oriented fig, ax = plt.subplots() style (not the pyplot shortcuts), recreate the lesson's 12-month revenue line chart with np.random.default_rng(7), then build the 5-panel bar/barh/hist/scatter/boxplot grid against a seeded 300-row customer table (groupby segment, spend, orders), labeling every axis with set_title/set_xlabel/set_ylabel and exporting the final figure with fig.savefig(..., dpi=130, bbox_inches="tight").
slots.deliverable: One saved PNG containing the reproduced revenue line chart plus the 5-chart-type grid (bar, barh, hist, scatter, boxplot), all built with the matplotlib object-oriented API and fully labeled.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the bar chart you built last slot and customize it: apply a deliberate palette with one highlighted accent color against greyed-out context bars, add data-value annotations above each bar, a custom legend, and at least one reference line via axhline (e.g. the group average), then export both a light-background and a dark-background version of the same figure.
slots.deliverable: One fully customized, annotated bar chart (highlight color, value labels, legend, reference line) exported as both a light-background and dark-background PNG.

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild the seeded 500-row customers table (age, region, channel, tenure_months, orders, total_spend, churned, with 20 planted missing ages and 2 planted outlier spend values) and use seaborn to build a histplot with a KDE overlay for total_spend, a boxplot of total_spend by region, and a pairplot of age/tenure_months/total_spend colored by churned, then write 2-3 sentences on what the boxplot reveals about spend differences across regions.
slots.deliverable: A seaborn histplot+KDE, a boxplot of spend by region, and a churn-colored pairplot of 3 numeric columns, plus a written 2-3 sentence interpretation of the regional spend difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild one of your matplotlib charts (the region-level spend comparison) as an interactive Plotly Express chart with hover tooltips showing the exact customer count and mean spend per region, then add a dropdown or range-slider style interaction (e.g. a Plotly animation_frame or a second trace toggled by legend click) and export the result as a standalone HTML file you can open and interact with in a browser.
slots.deliverable: One interactive Plotly HTML file with working hover tooltips and at least one additional interactive control (dropdown, slider, or toggleable legend trace).

slots.practicalActivity: Combine 4 of the charts you have built across this chapter (one distribution, one categorical comparison, one relationship/scatter, one time-based or grouped chart) into a single multi-panel dashboard using matplotlib's plt.subplots(2, 2) grid with a shared figure title, consistent color scheme across all 4 panels, and fig.tight_layout() so nothing overlaps.
slots.deliverable: One 2x2-panel dashboard figure combining 4 different chart types from this chapter with a shared title and consistent color scheme, exported as a single PNG.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate the lesson's seeded 500-row customers.csv (age, region, channel, tenure_months, orders, total_spend, churned, with 20 planted missing ages and 2 planted outlier spend values), write down 2-3 specific questions before looking at any chart, then run the first-look checks (shape, info(), isna().sum(), duplicated().sum(), churned.value_counts(normalize=True), describe()) and note in writing which number (mean vs. median gap on total_spend) first signals a problem worth chasing.
slots.deliverable: The generated customers.csv, 2-3 written pre-registered questions, and a first-look report (shape, missingness, duplicate count, churn balance, describe() output) with a written note identifying the mean-vs-median red flag.

slots.practicalActivity: On the same customers.csv, run a full univariate pass: histograms for age, tenure_months, orders, and total_spend; value_counts() bar charts for region and channel; and compute skewness for total_spend, deciding whether a log transform would make the distribution easier to read, then apply np.log1p to total_spend and compare the before/after histograms side by side.
slots.deliverable: A set of univariate histograms/bar charts for every column, a computed skewness value for total_spend, and a before/after side-by-side histogram showing the effect of a log transform.

slots.practicalActivity: On customers.csv, compare pairs of variables: a scatter of tenure_months vs. total_spend colored by churned, a grouped bar of mean total_spend by channel, and a crosstab of region vs. churned converted to row-percentages, then write 2-3 sentences naming the single clearest two-variable relationship you found and the actual numbers behind it.
slots.deliverable: A colored scatter plot, a grouped bar chart by channel, and a row-percentage crosstab of region by churn, plus a written 2-3 sentence summary of the strongest relationship found, citing real numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: On customers.csv, build a 3+ variable view: a seaborn FacetGrid or relplot of orders vs. total_spend split by region and colored by channel, and a groupby on two categorical columns at once (region and channel) aggregating mean churn rate and count, then check whether a bivariate pattern you found last slot still holds once you control for a third variable, writing down whether it strengthens, weakens, or disappears.
slots.deliverable: One multi-faceted relplot/FacetGrid split by 2 categorical variables, a two-way groupby aggregation table, and a written note on whether a previously found pattern holds after controlling for a third variable.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the full correlation matrix for the numeric columns in customers.csv with .corr(), render it as a seaborn heatmap with annotated values, identify the single strongest pair, and compute both Pearson and Spearman correlation for that pair to check whether the relationship is linear or just monotonic, writing a sentence on which one is more trustworthy for this pair and why.
slots.deliverable: An annotated correlation heatmap for all numeric columns, plus a written comparison of Pearson vs. Spearman correlation for the single strongest pair found.

slots.practicalActivity: On customers.csv, flag outliers in total_spend using the IQR method (below Q1-1.5*IQR or above Q3+1.5*IQR), confirm the 2 planted extreme spend values get caught, build a boxplot showing them, then make and justify a written decision for each flagged row: cap it, investigate it as a data-entry error, or keep it as a legitimate high-value customer.
slots.deliverable: An IQR-based outlier flag column with a printed count of flagged rows, a boxplot visualizing them, and a written keep/cap/investigate decision for each flagged outlier with a one-sentence justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Install ydata-profiling and Sweetviz, generate a full ProfileReport HTML and a Sweetviz analyze() HTML report on customers.csv, read every alert the tools surface, then write down one real finding the automated report caught that you had not already found by hand, and one thing it missed (e.g. it does not know that a $9,800 spend is implausible for this business) that only your own context-aware judgment caught.
slots.deliverable: Two generated HTML profiling reports (ydata-profiling and Sweetviz) on the same dataset, plus a written note naming one finding the tool caught and one it missed that required business context.

slots.practicalActivity: The EDA Workflow practice lab: pick a second real dataset you have not used in this course yet (a public Kaggle dataset or similar), and run the full 5-stage workflow end to end on it from scratch: frame a specific question, do the first-look checks, go univariate, then bivariate/multivariate, run a correlation heatmap and an IQR outlier check, and generate one automated profiling report, writing a short running list of every surprise you found along the way.
slots.deliverable: One complete EDA pass on a new real dataset covering all 5 workflow stages (question, first look, univariate, bivariate/multivariate, decide), plus a written running list of surprises found.

lessons.title: Connecting Power BI to Python & SQL Data

slots.practicalActivity: These 3 lessons reuse Power BI skills from the Power BI course at a lighter touch, so spend most of this hour building, not watching: in Power BI Desktop, load customers.csv via Get Data > Text/CSV (or use a Python script source per the lesson), build one exploratory report page with a region-by-churn-rate bar chart, a total_spend distribution, and a slicer on channel, then write down in plain language the one finding you would lead with if you only had 60 seconds with a stakeholder.
slots.deliverable: One Power BI report page connected to the customers dataset with at least 3 visuals and a working slicer, plus a written one-sentence lead finding for a stakeholder.

lessons.title: Telling the Story of a Dataset

slots.practicalActivity: Rebuild the lesson's seeded 800-row churn dataset (plan, region, tenure, support_tickets, churned), group churn rate by support_tickets clipped at 3+, confirm the ~4x churn-rate jump from 0 to 3+ tickets, build a single highlighted bar chart titled with the finding (not the variable names) using the one-accent-color technique, then write a half-page analysis following the context-tension-resolution structure, computing every number you state and showing the group sizes behind each rate.
slots.deliverable: One single-message highlighted bar chart titled with the actual finding, plus a half-page written analysis (context, tension, resolution) with every quoted number computed and every rate's underlying group size stated.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the churn finding from the previous slot, build a 4-slide deck following the answer-evidence-caveat-ask flow (one slide each), translate the ticket-to-churn relationship into plain language using both a frequency form ("about 1 in X") and a relative-plus-absolute comparison, write one caveat slide stating plainly that this is an association and not proof of causation, then deliver the pitch out loud to someone (or record yourself) in under 3 minutes.
slots.deliverable: A 4-slide deck (answer, evidence, caveat, ask) with the churn finding translated into plain-language frequencies, plus a timed under-3-minute delivery of the pitch to a real listener or recording.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Explore and Present a Real Dataset

slots.practicalActivity: Generate the capstone's seeded 800-row customer dataset (plan, region, tenure_months, monthly_spend with 12 planted missing values, support_tickets, churned), write a specific business question and the decision it informs in plain words (per the lesson's framing), then run the first-look checks and confirm the baseline churn rate of about 19.6%, or swap in a real dataset of your own choosing and repeat the same framing and first-look steps on it.
slots.deliverable: A framed business question and the decision it informs, written in plain words, plus a first-look report (shape, missingness, baseline outcome rate) on either the generated capstone dataset or your own chosen real dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Execute the full capstone pipeline on your chosen dataset: decide and apply a fix for any missing values, run a complete univariate-then-bivariate-then-multivariate pass tied to your stated question, build a correlation heatmap and an IQR outlier check, and produce one final, clearly titled, single-accent-color chart that carries your single strongest finding.
slots.deliverable: One complete, documented EDA notebook covering missing-data handling, univariate/bivariate/multivariate analysis, correlation and outlier checks, and one polished, finding-titled final chart.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-to-two-page portfolio summary of the capstone project in plain language (the question, the key numeric findings with every number computed, one honest limitation of the data or method, and a recommended next action), then package the notebook/script, final chart, and summary together as a single artifact you could show in a job interview.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written portfolio summary (question, findings, limitation, recommendation) packaged with the finished EDA notebook and final chart as one interview-ready artifact.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can take a raw tabular dataset and run it through the full exploratory analysis loop -- build the right chart for the right question in matplotlib, seaborn, and Plotly, run a disciplined univariate-through-multivariate EDA workflow with correlation and outlier checks, hand findings to a stakeholder in Power BI, and write and present an honest, evidence-backed analysis that a non-technical audience can act on.
